hints: Focus on the types of bonds shown in the structure and what atoms are joined by single versus multiple bonds.
Notice this is glucose in its ring form, where every C-C, C-O, C-H and O-H link drawn is a single bond.
Think about the shape around each tetrahedral, sp3 carbon and oxygen in the ring to decide if a six-membered saturated ring can stay flat.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the molecule**

This is glucose in its cyclic (pyranose) form, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$. It has a six-membered ring made of five C atoms and one O atom, with $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ side groups.

All the lines drawn represent single covalent bonds.

**Check for sigma versus pi bonds**

A single bond contains one $\sigma$ bond only. A double bond would contain one $\sigma$ plus one $\pi$ bond.

$$\text{single bond} = 1 \times \sigma \text{ only}$$

**Apply to this structure**

There are no C=C or C=O double bonds here. Every C-C, C-O, C-H and O-H bond is single, so statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is incorrect.

**Decide planar or non-planar**

Each ring carbon is bonded to four groups, so it is tetrahedral and $sp^3$ hybridised with bond angles near $109.5^{\circ}$. The ring oxygen is also $sp^3$ with two lone pairs.

Tetrahedral centres cannot all lie in one flat plane, so the ring puckers into a chair shape to reduce strain. Therefore statement 4 is correct and statement 3 is incorrect.

options.A: Statement 1 is correct because all bonds are single $\sigma$ bonds, but statement 3 is wrong. A saturated six-membered ring with tetrahedral sp3 carbons cannot be planar.
options.B: Statement 1 is correct as there are no double bonds, so only $\sigma$ bonds are present. Statement 4 is correct because tetrahedral C and O atoms force the ring into a puckered, non-planar chair conformation.
options.C: Both parts are wrong. Statement 2 is wrong because $\pi$ bonds need multiple bonds, which are absent. Statement 3 is wrong because sp3 centres prevent planarity.
options.D: Statement 4 is correct about non-planarity, but statement 2 is wrong. Students choosing this often assume the ring O or OH groups imply a C=O or pi character, but all bonds here are single.
